Title: A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/step-toward-defining-the-standard-model

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/step-toward-defining-the-standard-model/

Markdown Content:
The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an [October preprint⁠(opens in a new window)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09093) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

## What is missing from the Standard Model’s definition?

What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

## Left-handed particles

If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

But the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetr y. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

## An analogy with light and mirrors

To understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve said, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to _chirality_ when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s _helicity_, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.)

But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

If you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand.

There is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular.

A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson[1](https://openai.com/index/step-toward-defining-the-standard-model/#citation-bottom-1) worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger[2](https://openai.com/index/step-toward-defining-the-standard-model/#citation-bottom-2) built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher[3](https://openai.com/index/step-toward-defining-the-standard-model/#citation-bottom-3) showed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa[4](https://openai.com/index/step-toward-defining-the-standard-model/#citation-bottom-4) and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing.

## Getting the phase right

To identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another important property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one piling. The wave’s _phase_ is the stage of that rise and fall you catch it in when you look, perhaps just past its highest point and on its way down. For our circularly polarized light, the optical phase tracks the same kind of cycle at a fixed spot in the beam, with the electric field pointing up at the “crest” and down at the “trough.”

The relative phase of two waves determines how much they add or cancel at the same point. At one piling of a dock, two waves arriving in phase lift the water higher as their crests meet, while a crest arriving with a trough can leave the water close to its usual level. Similarly, light with the same phase in the same place builds up, while light with different phases can cancel out. In our box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light is now bouncing back and forth inside the box. After a lap, the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, they reinforce and the light builds up inside the box. If the fields are half a cycle apart, they point in opposite directions and the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. To build up a strong beam, we want the phase of each return to arrive in step with the source.

To get the phase right, we can rotate one chiral mirror relative to the other. Imagine a mark at twelve o’clock on the rim, and spin the mirror about the beam as though the beam were its axle. Title: Our new blog for science

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/our-new-blog-for-science

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/our-new-blog-for-science/

Markdown Content:
We’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:

*   **Research and discoveries:**New scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.

*   **Methods and practical guidance:** Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.

*   **Perspectives from the scientific community:** Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

Science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to new sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a [proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem⁠](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/), a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we [released a broad range of mathematical results⁠](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/). Among them was a result on the [quasi-Riemann hypothesis⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-September-30-2026/paper.pdf), with a result that gives a tighter bound on the error in a classical formula for estimating how many primes lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared [results across mathematics, computer science, and physics⁠](https://openai.com/index/building-scientific-understanding-with-academic-communities/) concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interacting quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab. [Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research⁠](https://openai.com/index/scaling-ai-research-for-complex-biological-data/), thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: [César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex⁠](https://openai.com/index/accelerating-antibiotic-discovery/) to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

These capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own.

# AI Day Seoul Brings Together Korea’s Industry Leaders, Startups and Developer Communities

November 15, 2026 by[NVIDIA Writers](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/nvidiawriters/ "Posts by NVIDIA Writers")

 Share

Share This Article

Over two days at COEX, more than 2,000 attendees converged for AI Day Seoul, bringing together Korea’s industry leaders, startups and developer communities advancing physical AI and AI agents.

At the plenary sessions, Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge AI at NVIDIA, said Korea is “punching above its weight,” with Doosan Robotics, Hyundai Motor Group, LG Electronics and SK Group — as well as startups like Real World and Luda Robotics — using NVIDIA platforms to bring general-purpose robotics into the real world.

Jonathan Cohen, vice president of applied research at NVIDIA, showed how enterprises can build agents they own and control. Breakout sessions featured speakers from Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Doosan Robotics, LG AI Research, LG Electronics, NAVER Cloud, SK Telecom and Upstage.

“It was a genuinely enjoyable time to have candid conversations,” said Hyunho Yang, research engineer for omnimodal foundation models at SK Telecom. “Seeing the passion of fellow AI developers was a real source of inspiration for me.”

Community leaders share how they build with open models and tools at AI Day Seoul.

The Agentic AI 10x Bootcamp Community Day brought together Pseudo Lab, Python Korea, PyTorchKR, HAERAE, Hugging Face KREW, Graph User Group, Womxn Who Code Korea, Dnol (Datayanolja) and other developer communities. Five finalists from the Hangul Day hackathon, co-hosted with Fastcampus, built agents trained on the Korean language and culture with the OpenShell runtime. The winning team, FlyGate, received an NVIDIA DGX Spark system.

More than 500 developers also took part in full-day[NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/training/) workshops and NVIDIA Certification exams in Korean. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the [NVIDIA Isaac](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac) platform and developing secure AI agents. articles.content:
Bharat Semi
, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.
The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.
India has
committed billions of dollars
to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.
The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.
Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.
Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.
The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.
The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.
Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.
“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.
In 2024, Bharat Semi
announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project
in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.
The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

articles.content:
We didn’t see this coming. Or at least,
I
didn’t — a week ago, when
I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation
into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.
On the latest episode of
TechCrunch’s Equity podcast
, Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”
“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”
Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are
many who’d still like to see him return
.) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can
listen to the whole episode here
.
Tim De Chant:
I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days.
Rebecca Bellan:
I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me  — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.
But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down
Anthony Ha:
Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as
special
as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.
And for most people, Jensen Huang
is
Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.
Rebecca:
I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.
But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.
So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.
Anthony:
I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.
Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.
And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.
But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.
Rebecca:
That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.
I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.
I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that  — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.
Tim:
I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that
Nvidia’s head attorney had some role
in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.
Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.
Anthony:
There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.
People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.
Rebecca:
Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?
Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a
recurring
theme
on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.
Huang’s
ouster from Nvidia
(after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have
serious implications for the tech industry
; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.
In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”
Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about
flights being halted all across the United States
on Friday night.
“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of
Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday
. When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”
“Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”

Title: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 doesn't generate images, it paints them

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-claude-fable-5-2-doesnt-generate-images-it-paints-them/

Published Time: 2026-11-15T15:42:03+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Anthropic's new language model Claude Fable 5.2 can create complex and even photorealistic paintings by using code to place hundreds of thousands of individual brushstrokes on a virtual canvas.**

Current image models like Midjourney typically use diffusion, which gradually refines a noisy image into a clear result. [Fable 5.2](https://the-decoder.com/claude-fable-5-2-and-mythos-5-2-cement-anthropics-ai-lead-just-before-its-ipo/) takes a different approach by simulating the physical painting process, including bristle texture, how the paint goes on, and mistakes it then has to paint over.

Developer [Jake Eaton](https://x.com/jkeatn/status/2119874007382299087) showed on X what the approach can do. Eaton works at Anthropic, where he regularly contributes to research on language model values, safety mechanisms, and AI agent behavior.

When he asked [Fable 5.2](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2) to create a painting as hard to distinguish from a photograph as possible, the model generated an image of a shopping cart in a parking garage using roughly 700,000 simulated brushstrokes.

About 700,000 simulated brushstrokes went into this photorealistic parking garage scene by Claude Fable 5.2. | Image: Jake Eaton

According to Eaton, Claude works without an external image model and without pre-rendered or traced source images. Each piece is a Python program of 1,000 to 2,000 lines that drives a simulated paint engine. The approach resembles [agentic image editing](https://the-decoder.com/adobe-is-testing-how-well-ai-agents-can-use-editing-tools-like-a-photoshop-professional-would/?cmpscreencustom=1), where language models pick tools and evaluate results.

Earlier attempts with the sibling model Opus 5.5 drew criticism for merely imitating existing art. Eaton responded by having Fable 5.2 develop its own artist personas with fictional backstories and consistent styles. The model needs several thousand brushstrokes per painting, and Eaton redirects them with comments.

For its paintings, Fable 5.2 develops its own artist personas and controls brushwork through Python code. | Image: Jake Eaton

## Without an undo button, the model has to commit to every stroke

Anthropic engineer Michael Graczyk shared a [chat log and video](https://x.com/mgrczyk/status/2119943813028548721) of an experiment in which he asked Fable 5.2 to paint a bird at sunrise. The model could only use code to simulate the physics of bristles, wet paint, and canvas texture. It had to output every brushstroke manually as its own coordinate line, with no way to undo strokes once placed. That's what sets this method apart from AI-generated videos, where models like [Flux 3](https://the-decoder.com/flux-3-generates-videos-with-native-audio-up-to-20-seconds-long-a-first-for-black-forest-labs/) generate image sequences and their temporal consistency directly.

The resulting 21-second video uses a counter to track how the painting takes shape from exactly 111 strokes on a blank canvas. For the first stroke, the model output the color code `#30346a`, a width of 90 pixels, and five slightly wobbling waypoints. Fable 5.2 said it added the roughly seven-pixel wobble on purpose because a human arm doesn't draw a perfectly straight line either.

Between passes, the model looked at the canvas and reacted to its own mistakes like a real painter would. When the bird's back came out too thin and scraggly, the AI laid a bolder stroke over it, so the stray bristle marks along the edges now look like ruffled feathers.

In a second, 280-stroke piece showing two people painting at dusk, a late lighting effect accidentally smeared paint tubes and a cup on the table. Claude repainted those objects after the fact. The model also had both figures paint with their outer hands so their inner shoulders could touch, just as the prompt requested.

Even complex perspectives and lighting are handled by the language model through thousands of individual code instructions. | Image: Jake Eaton

## The same spatial reasoning transfers to physical robots

Fable 5.2's ability to plan step by step and self-correct under physical constraints isn't limited to virtual canvases. According to Anthropic, the model is built for extremely demanding long-horizon technical tasks, as is Mythos 5.2, a version designed for verified security and biology researchers.

In internal tests, Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in black hole physics, designed three working electronic devices with circuit board manufacturer Diode, and used more than 1,000 sub-agents to program its own laptop operating system in eight days.

[AI researcher Aris Zhu](https://x.com/ariszotle/status/2119945328917196825) tested how the model performs with real robotic arms. He pitted Fable 5.2 against OpenAI's competing model GPT-6 Astra, with each using a physical robot arm to paint Van Gogh's "The Starry Night." Anthropic reports a score of 64.9 percent for Fable 5.2 on its internal RoboDojo Sim benchmark, compared with 29.8 percent for GPT-6 Astra.

Zhu's real-world comparison still shows limits in fine motor control. Astra painted faster, and so far only OpenAI's model has managed to stand a domino on end. It did so by slowly loosening its gripper to use gravity as a pivot point.

Title: Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/australias-central-bank-finds-ai-hitting-young-workers-first-especially-in-software-and-customer-service/

Published Time: 2026-11-15T10:45:58+00:00

Markdown Content:
**AI has barely displaced any jobs in Australia so far, but young workers entering highly exposed fields like software development are faring worse.**

An analysis by Mike Major for Australia's central bank (RBA) built a monitoring system that focuses on the areas where effects are likely to appear first, namely entry-level workers and [highly AI-exposed occupations](https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-new-study-shows-ai-is-nowhere-near-its-theoretical-job-disruption-potential/) such as [programming](https://the-decoder.de/ki-uebernimmt-freelancer-jobs-texter-coder-und-grafiker-sind-besonders-betroffen/), clerical work, and customer service.

[According to the analysis](https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/insights/australian-economy/2026/monitoring-early-effects-of-ai-on-the-labour-market.html), job postings have fallen across all groups since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, with the steepest drop in the highest-exposure group. In that group, workers aged 15 to 24 and young college graduates have [weaker employment rates](https://the-decoder.com/the-tragedy-of-the-cognitive-commons-explains-how-rational-ai-adoption-could-destroy-entire-professions-expertise/) and higher unemployment than older workers.

In jobs with high potential AI exposure (quintile 5), employment among young people has declined since late 2022, while employment among older workers has risen. | Source: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA)

Major cautions against drawing early conclusions, since the study does not establish direct causation and measures only theoretical exposure, not actual use by companies. Post-pandemic shifts in the business cycle or in remote work could also be driving the numbers. According to SEEK data, AI is complementing existing work while also creating [new demand for AI skills](https://the-decoder.com/uks-job-market-is-splitting-in-two-as-ai-demand-surges-while-knowledge-work-postings-crater/?cmpscreencustom=1).

## Other studies paint a similar picture, with caveats

An August 2025 [Stanford study based on millions of US payroll records](https://the-decoder.com/ai-tools-like-chatgpt-sharply-reduce-jobs-for-young-workers-in-exposed-fields-stanford-study-shows/) found a similar pattern, with employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations down 13 percent in relative terms since late 2022 and nearly 20 percent among young software developers. More experienced workers in the same occupations held steady or gained ground.

A [March 2026 Anthropic study](https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-new-study-shows-ai-is-nowhere-near-its-theoretical-job-disruption-potential/) also found signs of declining hiring among 22- to 25-year-olds in exposed occupations, with job-finding rates down about 14 percent. It found no systematic rise in overall unemployment, however. Theoretical automation potential and actual AI use are far apart, according to the study.

Anthropic offers a company-level example. According to an [internal review](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-has-nearly-stopped-hiring-junior-staff-because-ai-agents-now-work-six-times-as-many-hours/), the share of junior hires in technical roles has fallen from 27 percent to 9 percent since early 2025. In August 2026, AI agents across the company were already logging six times as many hours as human employees. Anthropic concedes that, as an extremely AI-intensive software company, it is a special case. Even so, researchers warn of a ["tragedy of the cognitive commons"](https://the-decoder.com/the-tragedy-of-the-cognitive-commons-explains-how-rational-ai-adoption-could-destroy-entire-professions-expertise/), in which disappearing junior roles lead to a future shortage of experienced professionals, assuming those professionals are still needed.

A [large study of 25,000 workers in Denmark](https://the-decoder.com/chatbots-like-chatgpt-have-not-led-to-significant-changes-in-wages-or-working-hours-study-finds/) confirms the lack of economy-wide impact. Despite a 64 percent AI adoption rate, researchers found no measurable changes in wages or hours worked. Workers saved an average of just 2.8 percent of their working time.

A January 2026 [analysis of 10.6 million LinkedIn profiles and US unemployment data](https://the-decoder.com/new-study-disrupts-the-narrative-that-chatgpts-launch-triggered-a-job-decline/), however, cautions against blaming the downturn on AI alone. The research team led by Morgan Frank at the University of Pittsburgh found that the problems in exposed occupations started in early 2022, months before ChatGPT launched. Macroeconomic factors like the Fed's shift in interest rate policy or a correction after pandemic-era hiring surges may play a bigger role than previously assumed.

At the same time, AI is creating new demand. According to the World Economic Forum's ["Future of Jobs Report 2025"](https://the-decoder.com/companies-prioritize-ai-training-over-job-cuts-wef-study-finds/), 77 percent of surveyed companies are prioritizing upskilling over job cuts. WEF researchers project a net gain of 78 million jobs by 2030. [According to LinkedIn](https://the-decoder.com/ai-job-postings-on-linkedin-grew-sixfold-as-ai-skill-additions-to-profiles-soared-twentyfold/), AI-related job postings grew sixfold in one year.

Title: Meituan releases a 1.6-trillion-parameter agent model that never touched an Nvidia GPU

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/meituan-releases-a-1-6-trillion-parameter-agent-model-that-never-touched-an-nvidia-gpu/

Published Time: 2026-11-15T10:06:06+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Meituan releases the weights for LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model built for AI agents. It was trained entirely on Chinese hardware and performs at the level US models like Claude Opus 5 reached a few months ago on coding benchmarks.**

The LongCat team at Chinese food delivery company Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, one week after the model's official unveiling. LongCat-2.5 is built for agents that work through long, multi-step tasks autonomously, particularly coding. According to Meituan, it comes close to top Western models on several benchmarks.

LongCat-2.5 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates only a subset of its specialized subnetworks for each token it processes. Out of 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion are active per token. Through the API, the model handles up to one million tokens at once and generates responses up to 128,000 tokens long. It understands text, images, and video, responds in text, and lets users toggle reasoning on and off.

## LongCat-2.5 converts images into tokens

LongCat-2.5 builds on its [predecessor LongCat-2.0](https://the-decoder.com/meituans-longcat-2-0-shows-china-can-train-massive-ai-models-without-nvidia/) and adds image understanding. Many multimodal models bolt on a separate image encoder after the fact. LongCat-2.5 instead converts images into tokens that the model processes alongside text, as is standard practice for today's LLMs. The approach draws on the research model LongCat-Next and aims to improve visual coding, design, and 3D tasks.

LongCat-2.5 breaks images down at their native resolution into discrete tokens that the model processes alongside text. | Image: Meituan

For reinforcement learning, the team used real software tasks from GitHub pull requests along with recreated agent failures. To make sure the model actually solved the tasks during training, the developers blocked internet access in the training environments, removed Git history and cached files, and had a language model check its solutions for tricks. The team also distilled the capabilities of several specialized teacher models for agent work, reasoning, and dialog into LongCat-2.5.

Meituan generates training tasks from real GitHub repositories and blocks shortcuts like web search and Git history in the sandbox. | Image: Meituan

## A sample deployment runs on 194 Huawei chips

Meituan quantizes the experts' weights and activations to 4-bit precision, which Chinese chips can process natively. In Meituan's load tests, throughput rises 43.3 percent for prompt processing and 42.77 percent for response generation compared with an 8-bit version. Meituan says accuracy stays on par with the uncompressed model.

This version is available in a [separate repository](https://huggingface.co/meituan-longcat/LongCat-2.5-W4A4). The [self-hosting guide](https://github.com/meituan-longcat/SGLang-FluentLLM/blob/longcat-2.5-npu/npu_test/ReadMe.md) describes a cluster of 194 [Huawei Ascend accelerators](https://the-decoder.com/chinas-ai-strategy-huawei-focuses-on-system-size-not-chip-efficiency/) from the Atlas A2 series. Two handle image processing, 64 handle prompt ingestion, and 128 handle response generation. There's no guidance for Nvidia GPUs.

## LongCat-2.5 trails Opus 5 slightly on terminal tasks

The LongCat team reports 88.4 points on Terminal Bench v2.1, a benchmark that measures how well agents solve command-line tasks. Meituan lists [Claude Opus 5](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-claims-its-new-claude-opus-5-delivers-near-fable-5-performance-at-half-the-token-price/) at 89.1, [GPT-5.6 Sol](https://the-decoder.com/openais-claude-mythos-competitor-gpt-5-6-sol-launches-under-government-controlled-access-it-calls-unsustainable/) at 88.8, and [Deepseek-V4.1-Flash](https://the-decoder.com/new-deepseek-model-v4-1-flash-cuts-memory-needs-for-ai-agents/) at the top of the table with 90.6.

DeepSWE tests how well models fix bugs in real code repositories. Here LongCat-2.5 jumps from 9.7 to 64.6 points, placing it behind every other model in the table except [Claude Opus 4.8](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ships-claude-opus-4-8-as-a-modest-but-tangible-improvement-that-tops-gpt-5-5-in-most-benchmarks/), with Deepseek-V4.1-Flash leading at 74.2 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 72.7. The more recent [Claude Opus 5.5](https://the-decoder.com/claude-opus-5-5-matches-fable-5-1-at-40-percent-lower-cost-as-anthropic-promises-to-fix-claudish-writing/) and [GPT-6.1 Sol](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-1-sol-comes-close-to-astra-at-a-fifth-of-the-price/) are not included in the table.

In Meituan's own evaluation, LongCat-2.5 improves substantially over its predecessor and comes close to Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on several agent benchmarks. | Image: Meituan

Terminal Bench v4.0, the harder variant, puts LongCat-2.5 at 38.5 points, slightly above GPT-5.6 Sol's 37.3 but well below Opus 5's 53.9. The model posts 91.9 on the web search benchmark BrowseComp, the highest score in the table, though Meituan ran this test in its own environment.

The [weights are available](https://huggingface.co/meituan-longcat/LongCat-2.5) under the MIT license, which allows commercial use, modification, and redistribution. Users can also try LongCat-2.5 in a chat interface at [https://longcat.ai/](https://longcat.ai/). Its API supports both the OpenAI and Anthropic formats and plugs into agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes. At launch, Meituan is charging a limited-time promotional price equivalent to roughly €0.27 per million input tokens and €1.07 per million output tokens.

Meituan says it trained the predecessor LongCat-2.0 in late June [entirely on a cluster of more than 50,000 Chinese AI chips](https://the-decoder.com/meituans-longcat-2-0-shows-china-can-train-massive-ai-models-without-nvidia/). Before that, the model ran anonymously as "Owl Alpha" on OpenRouter. Chinese open-weight models like [Kimi K3.1](https://the-decoder.com/chinese-ai-model-kimi-k3-1-pro-is-closing-in-on-anthropics-claude-opus-5-5/) and [GLM-5.3](https://the-decoder.com/the-chinese-ai-model-glm-5-3-flash-runs-without-nvidia-and-costs-a-fraction-of-what-the-competition-does/) have largely caught up with top US models on common benchmarks.

Open-weight models optimized for Chinese chips from the start make that [hardware more attractive outside China too](https://the-decoder.com/frontier-radar-4-china-has-caught-up-so-whats-left-of-the-western-ai-lead/). Beyond multimodal agent models, Meituan is also working on image generators. The company previously [released LongCat-Image, an open-source text-to-image model](https://the-decoder.com/longcat-image-proves-6b-parameters-can-beat-bigger-models-with-better-data-hygiene/) that gets by with just 6 billion parameters and prioritizes efficiency over sheer model size.

What is Tofu-1?
Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the
first release in a planned family
of Bland speech-to-speech models.
How does Tofu-1 differ from a cascade voice agent?
Most voice agents are cascades. They turn speech into text, pass it to a language model, then turn the reply back into speech.
Tofu-1 listens to the audio directly
, so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland has not published the internal architecture.
Audio understanding
Bland lists 3 audio skills on its product page:
Speaker tracking:
tells speakers apart and works out who each one is addressing.
Noise separation:
separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones.
Paralinguistics:
hears hesitation, frustration and urgency.
Full duplex and thinking while talking
Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early.
Scene generation
Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise.
What is Bland’s ‘TV Test’?
The TV Test asks one question: can the model follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene? TV audio is often louder than the caller. Bland marks its TV Test walkthrough as illustrative, not recorded model output.

Title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs

URL Source: https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-positional-embeddings

Published Time: 2026-11-15T12:10:37+00:00

Markdown Content:
This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my [LLM gallery](https://sebastianraschka.com/llm-architecture-gallery/).

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

*   different positional methods in LLMs;

*   (finally) how RoPE works;

*   what methods are used by recent open LLMs.

Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to [Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)](https://sebastianraschka.com/books/#build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my [self-attention walkthrough](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-and-coding-self-attention) as a refresher:

The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.

**PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added [image exports and metadata](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/perks) from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.**

PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, _Positional choices in modern architectures_.

Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the [web view here](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-positional-embeddings), which also has a navigation bar on the left side.

Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.

The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.

Figure 2: Token embedding layers in GPT-2 and MiniMax-M3, highlighted in orange. (Side note: M3’s first three out of 60 feedforward layers are dense not MoEs.)

A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.

We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.

Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:

1.   “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”

2.   “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”

Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.

Figure 3: Changing the word order changes which fox jumps.

For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.

Figure 4: Token IDs and positions in the toy sentence.

(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my [tokenizer materials on GitHub](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/tree/main/ch02/05_bpe-from-scratch).)

Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer.

Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.

GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.)

Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information.

If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article.

We briefly talked about _implicit_ positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the _explicit_ ways to add positional information.

The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections.

To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block.

Figure 5: GPT-2 adds absolute position information before the transformer blocks, as highlighted in purple. The dimensions shown are for [GPT-2 XL](https://huggingface.co/openai-community/gpt2-xl/blob/main/config.json).

The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation:

And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let _m_ be a position index and _x m_ the token ID at that position. The input to the first block is

Here,

*   _E_ token is the embedding layer,

*   _P m_ is the position info vector selected by _m_,

*   and _h m_ is the resulting summed embedding and position vector.

The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise. Figure 6 below shows this visually with a small numerical example.

Figure 6: Token and position embeddings are added element-wise. (I am following the convention here that neural network diagrams are usually read from bottom to top.)

In the figure above, at position 0, adding the token embedding `[1, 1, 1]` to the position embedding `[1.1, 1.2, 1.3]` gives `[2.1, 2.2, 2.3]`. By the way, the values in the figure are chosen to keep the illustration simple; in a real example, both embedding layers (tables) are initialized with small random values and learned during training.

So, what we covered in this section is a so-called _absolute_ positional method because the positional embedding _P m_ depends on the token’s own position _m_. In the previous example sentence, the two “fox” tokens have initially the same token embeddings, but because we are adding different positional vectors _P 2_ and _P 7_, they have different values before they enter the first transformer block. And consequently, the query, key, and value vectors inside the attention mechanisms then also receive representations that already include position information.

Note that the original [GPT-2 implementation](https://github.com/openai/gpt-2/blob/master/src/model.py) has 1,024 learned position vectors. This means it only works with inputs with 1024 or fewer tokens. If we want to extend the context window, we would have to extend this embedding table. And since the embedding table (layer) is updated like any other layer during training, the context length would have to be decided before the training starts.

Extending the context would be very expensive since the table can become very large. For example, in the case of GPT-2 Medium, the positional embedding layer weights only make up 0.30% of the total weights at 1,024 positions. However, if we increased the context length to a nowadays common 100k range, they would make up >22% of the total model weights, which would be very uneconomic.

The original [“Attention Is All You Need”](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) transformer from 2017, which predates GPT, uses the same addition mechanism, but computes its position vectors with fixed sine and cosine functions. Figure 7 below shows this addition before both the encoder and decoder stacks. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder generates the output sequence. (The reason why it’s introduced here is that the sine and cosine functions will become relevant again later when discussing RoPE.)

Figure 7: Sinusoidal position encodings added to the token embeddings as highlighted in purple.

Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
This is
The Stepback
, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on Jensen Huang’s resignation and the fallout from Nvidia’s leadership crisis,
follow Terrence O’Brien
.
The Stepback
arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for
The Stepback
here
.
How it started
On October 29th,
The New York Times
reported that Nvidia co-founder and
showman
CEO Jensen Huang
appeared to be the target
of a Chinese spy plot. Any major tech CEO potentially being compromised by the Chinese government is concerning — especially Jensen Huang. “If you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that,” Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, previously
told
The Verge
. “If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.”
The
Times
reported that Jensen Huang had developed a “
close relationship
” with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. Alice Huang had been on the American government’s radar for some time, perhaps
as early as 2024
. Her company was investigated by the US Commerce Department over suspicions it was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China in violation of US government trade restrictions. Singapore authorities
confiscated her passport
back in June of 2025, eventually barring her from the country, after she reportedly gave “inaccurate information” to police. And perhaps more concerningly, some US officials believed she was passing information, possibly about Nvidia’s designs or the White House’s deliberations over trade restrictions, directly back to Beijing.
This made her relationship with Jensen Huang concerning for multiple reasons. Nvidia’s chips are considered crucial to America’s AI superiority and a matter of national security by the White House. The government has restricted the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China since the Biden administration. But Jensen Huang has routinely pushed to
loosen those trade restrictions
. Meanwhile, he had gotten quite cozy with President Trump, once even
putting him on speakerphone
on-stage at the All-In Summit.
Then last week, things escalated quickly.
On Friday, November 6th, the
Times
reported that Alice Huang was specifically
recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security
to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Though, there is
some disagreement
among US intelligence officials over the strength of evidence tying Alice Huang to Beijing. While the paper did not confirm it at the time, rumors suggested the “close relationship” between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang was romantic in nature.
On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang
admitted
to having an extramarital affair, but did not name the Megaspeed exec and alleged Chinese spy specifically. Nvidia’s board announced that it was
launching an investigation
into its CEO shortly after.
Many
believed
that Jensen Huang would
survive
the scandal. His company’s importance to America’s booming AI industry and his crucial role at the company seemed to make him nearly untouchable. He was, after all, the only CEO the company had ever known with no clear and obvious succession plan in place, and he sat atop an unusual corporate structure with around 60 direct reports. (These numbers are slightly outdated, but according to the
Harvard Business Review
,
10 to 20 is far more common
among Fortune 500 companies, and Tim Cook
reportedly had 17 in 2015
, which was deemed “a lot” by
Business Insider
.)
Then on Wednesday, November 11th,
The New York Times
reported
that Jensen Huang had a second affair — this one with one of his direct reports, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Whether that was the last straw or if they were afraid it would be merely the tip of the iceberg, the board was ready to
push Jensen Huang out,
according to reports circulating that evening. According to
Bloomberg
, he had accepted his fate Wednesday evening reportedly looking “broken and shattered” and telling people, “I’m a piece of shit.”
On Thursday, November 12th, Nvidia announced that
Jensen Huang had resigned
as CEO of Nvidia.
How it’s going
CFO Colette Kress was immediately named interim CEO, and acknowledged to employees that this has been an “
extraordinarily difficult period
.” Harvey Jones was also named the first board chair in the company’s history, already signaling there would be some changes to the corporate structure. In a memo to employees, Jones said the company would “search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates.”
But the destabilizing impact was immediate. Nvidia’s stock closed at an all-time high of
$239.24 on October 6th
. It closed at
$162.85
on November 13th. It’s hard to overstate the importance of Nvidia to the US’s
AI arms race with China
, and the industry in general. The company has invested
$99 billion
in various AI labs, startups, and neo clouds. Plus has announced plans to mobilize
over $500 billion
in financing for building out AI data centers and other infrastructure.
Even before Jensen Huang had resigned, Nvidia was already facing a
shareholder lawsuit
claiming the company had deceived investors. Jensen Huang and the company’s spokespeople insisted that the relationship with Alice Huang and Megaspeed was “
completely normal and not unusual
.” Only days later, Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair that raised “
national security concerns
” without naming anyone specifically. According to
Reuters
, Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, “including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld” about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang.
Many in the AI industry and Silicon Valley
jumped to Jensen Huang’s defense
. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it a “
sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity
,” in a particularly hyperbolic post. Elon Musk said on X that it would “
be an honor
” to hire Jensen Huang. Many of Nvidia’s employees even voiced their support to “
bring back THE boss
,” on an internal post.
Some even speculated that Jensen Huang was the victim of a
vast conspiracy
, whether that was a coup by some faction within Nvidia, or perhaps the goal of China all along had simply been to
chase him from the CEO chair
.
By Thursday night, Reuters reported a
third affair
, this one also with an Nvidia employee, though no further information has emerged.
What happens next
First and foremost for Nvidia, it must find a new CEO. It’s possible that Kress eventually ceases to be “interim” CEO, but other names, including Apple’s hardware chief
Johny Srouji
, have also been rumored. (Donald Trump believes they should hire
Tim Cook
, but to call that unlikely would be an understatement.)
It’s also possible that Nvidia will undergo a dramatic reorganization. Whoever takes over as CEO is unlikely to keep the 60 direct reports of Jensen Huang. With a first-ever board chair in Jones, it’s also possible that the board of directors will play a larger role in the company going forward.
The board’s investigation into Jensen Huang that began on November 8th is ongoing. The scandal is
likely to drag on for some time
. With the possibility that Jensen Huang will have to
testify before Congress
, the company may choose to be proactive about disclosing any additional information publicly.
The incoming Democratic majority is expected to come down harder on Silicon Valley than the current Republican Congress. While it’s unclear just how far the new House and Senate will go in trying to rein in the tech industry and its billionaire leaders, it’s possible it will try to make an example of Nvidia as an early act of strength. If Nvidia is found to have been turning a blind eye to companies like Megaspeed, which are suspected of funneling advanced chips to China, it could face civil or criminal penalties. And it seems increasingly likely that stricter trade restrictions will be implemented on Nvidia’s chips, which could increase tensions with China in an already costly trade war.
There is a possibility that Jensen Huang could face criminal charges. In May, he claimed that Nvidia had “
zero percent
” market share in China due to stringent export restrictions. But shortly after, Culper Research published a report claiming that in reality
over 20 percent
of the company’s 2026 compute revenue was from China, though that number has not been independently verified. The report cited “illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries” as the primary source of those revenues. Among the largest of those intermediaries, according to Culper Research, was Megaspeed, which Nvidia repeatedly vouched for to the US government.
If proof is established that the CEO was knowingly helping Megaspeed or any other companies to illegally divert restricted chips to China, he could face criminal charges. And, as
The Verge’s
Elizabeth Lopatto put it, “under a functioning legal system, [he]
could actually go to jail
.”
There is the chance that members of the current administration are also tied up in this scandal, as it’s unclear
how much the White House knew and when
.
Considering Nvidia’s sizable investments, borrowing to build data centers, and the importance of its hardware, there are tons of open questions about how this impacts not just the AI industry, but the American economy as a whole. Nvidia is essentially
propping up
a large part of the tech industry and, if money stops flowing out of its coffers, it could drag a lot of other companies down with it.
There are also open questions about how this impacts the American public’s perception of the AI industry. The new Democratic majority was elected in part by
campaigning against AI companies
and the explosion of data center buildout across the country. That one of its more prominent CEOs is now embroiled in a spying scandal and multiple extramarital affairs probably isn’t going to endear the industry to the public.
By the way
Megaspeed was the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia, but when Singaporean newspaper
The Straits Times
visited its office in October of 2025, it found “no signs of activity.”
Megaspeed is just one of multiple companies that Nvidia has been approved to sell chips with suspicious offices.
The New York Times
described New Matrix’s headquarters as “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.”
Jensen Huang’s connections to Super Micro are also under scrutiny. Earlier this year,
one of its founders
, an employee, and
a contractor
for the company were
indicted
by the Justice Department for conspiring to violate American export controls and divert Nvidia chips to China.
Read this
While a lot has changed, it’s still worth reading the
Times
’ first big report from October 29th that lays the groundwork for the eventual deluge of international intrigue and infidelity that ultimately led to Jensen Huang’s downfall.
The New York Times
paints a fascinating portrait of Alice Huang who now finds herself at the center of an international espionage scandal.

interview with
Kyle Chan
, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution

Andrew Liszewski

Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with
OpenEvidence
, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like
The New England Journal of Medicine
. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance.
The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.
Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence.
Participants in the study will be given the opportunity to rate responses to health questions from the app.
Image: Apple
During enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models. The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

Title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source

URL Source: https://jakub.jankiewicz.org/blog/ai-code-open-source/

Markdown Content:
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.

First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.

The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous [Monkey Selfie dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey_selfie_copyright_dispute), which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, [Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Commons:AI-generated_media).

However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.

Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.

If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: [@jcubic](https://jcu.bi/twitter) and on [LinkedIn](https://jcu.bi/ln).

See [hacker news for discussion](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50507303)
